title: What I Learned at EDUCAUSE about the Higher Ed AI Conversation(s) Part 1
author: Lance Eaton
summary: Lance Eaton reports back from his first EDUCAUSE conference, using it to map the conversations higher education was having about generative AI eleven months after ChatGPT launched. He observes that everyone was asking who is using AI and for what, yet few institutions had launched anything, with the University of Michigan's internal tool the standout. He notes that no central place exists to share what institutions are actually doing, which risks endless reinventing of wheels. He then takes up a panel question, whether institutions need new AI policy or just usage guidance, and argues they need all three: new policy, adjusted existing policy such as academic integrity and FERPA, and practical usage guidance. His case for policy rests on the fact that generative AI automates the creation of content, which is the core work higher education prides itself on.
points: Institutions need to develop generative AI policy, adjust existing policy, and write usage guidance, rather than treating them as alternatives.
Academic integrity policies written around paper mills and copying leave gaps that generative AI exploits, so their language must be updated explicitly.
There is no central, comprehensive record of what institutions are actually doing with AI, which fuels duplicated effort and slow progress.
Because AI produces knowledge-like content, it touches the identity of higher education as knowledge creator, which justifies dedicated policy.
Staff, researchers, teachers and students have different assumptions and uses, so a single institutional stance cannot fit all.
quotes: Everyone wanted to know about everyone else: who was using AI, what were they using, and what for. It felt a bit like a frenzied “show me yours and I’ll show you mine.”—Often to find that most of us had very little to show.
Without some central space to share these kinds of updates, I think there’s going to be a lot of reinventing of wheels—which is the thing that contributes to institutions being so slow.

An institution has many components and not all of them operate under the same assumptions, motivations, values, or practices. How a university board may look to use or want AI used in the institution is going to be different from marketing to funding and development to admissions to student support.
This is part of the challenge. Institutions need to do all three as far as I see it: Develop generative AI policy, adjust existing policy, and develop usage guidance.

Adjusting existing policy also makes sense. For instance, this is what many colleges have done with their academic integrity policies. The language of such policies often did not include the language around generative AI. For instance, they would have language around acquiring a written paper through a paper mill or taking the words of another person. Generative AI is neither of these things so a student could make a technical argument.

There are also places where it’s self-evident that it exists and institutions just need to point to it clearly and loudly. FERPA, the law protecting the privacy of students is a good example where we can say unequivocally that generative AI falls under these laws and faculty should not enter private information of students into any generative AI.

Higher education is THE knowledge worker—creators and disseminators of knowledge. A new tool has arisen that appears to have similar and relevant abilities to produce information or content (some will argue knowledge—not sure I’m there yet) that feels strikingly similar to knowledge.
